entry: Mapping of an abstract group into the invertible linear transformations of a vector space. In mathematics, group representations describe abstract groups in terms of bijective linear transformations of a vector space to itself, so that group elements can be written as invertible matrices and the group operation as matrix multiplication. This reduces many problems in [[Group theory|group theory]] to problems in [[Linear algebra|linear algebra]]. In [[Physics|physics]], representations describe how the symmetry group of a system affects the solutions of the equations that describe it; in chemistry, they relate group elements to the rotations and reflections of molecules. For finite groups, many results are proved by averaging over the group. The same methods extend to locally compact groups, forming a central part of [[Harmonic analysis|harmonic analysis]], while Lie groups have their own techniques.

Sexual activity involving more than two participants. Any form of sexual activity can be adapted to involve more than two people, and some forms have their own names, such as [[Threesome|threesome]] and [[Gang bang|gang bang]]. Group sex most commonly takes place at private sex parties or semi-public swinger gatherings, but also at massage parlors, [[Brothel|brothels]] and, in some jurisdictions, purpose-built sex clubs. Participants may be of any [[Sexual orientation|sexual orientation]] or gender. Fantasies of group sex are extremely common among both men and women. It is a popular subgenre in [[Pornographic film|pornographic films]].

Branch of mathematics that studies the properties of groups. In [[Abstract algebra|abstract algebra]], group theory studies the algebraic structures known as groups. Other structures, such as rings, fields and vector spaces, can be seen as groups with additional operations and axioms. Symmetry groups model physical systems, including crystals, the [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]] atom and three of the four known fundamental forces, which makes the theory important in [[Physics|physics]], [[Chemistry|chemistry]] and [[Materials science|materials science]]. It is also central to public key cryptography. The theory has roots in number theory, the theory of algebraic equations and geometry; [[Évariste Galois|Évariste Galois]] coined the term "group". A collaborative effort, mostly published between 1960 and 2004 and running to more than 10,000 journal pages, produced a complete classification of finite simple groups.

Diverse group of marine ray-finned fishes in the family Epinephelidae, order [[Perciformes|Perciformes]]. Groupers were long considered a subfamily of the [[Serranidae|seabasses]] but are now treated as a distinct family. The word on its own usually refers to the large genera Epinephelus and Mycteroperca. Groupers are stout-bodied and not built for fast swimming, but some grow very large: the Atlantic goliath grouper has been weighed at 399 kilograms and measured 2.43 m. They swallow prey rather than biting off pieces, using heavy crushing tooth plates in the pharynx, and mostly eat fish, octopuses and [[Crustacean|crustaceans]]. Most are protogynous hermaphrodites: they mature as females and can later change sex. Groupers are also among the few animals that eat the invasive red lionfish.

Stocky, ground-dwelling birds of the tribe Tetraonini, in the order [[Galliformes|Galliformes]]. Grouse are classified in the family Phasianidae. The [[Turkey (bird)|turkeys]] are closely allied with grouse and may be treated as grouse in recent classifications. Grouse inhabit temperate and subarctic regions of the [[Northern Hemisphere|Northern Hemisphere]], from arctic [[Tundra|tundra]] to pine forests and moorland. True grouse range from 31 to 115 cm long and weigh 0.3 to 6.5 kg. Males are significantly larger than females and often have crests, fan-tails and inflatable patches of bare skin. Grouse feed mainly on vegetation: buds, catkins, leaves and twigs make up over 95% of adults' food by weight, and forest species eat large quantities of [[Conifer|conifer]] needles. Hatchlings eat mostly insects and other [[Invertebrate|invertebrates]]. Tundra ptarmigans form flocks of up to 300 or more in winter. All grouse spend most of their time on the ground.

American politician, 22nd and 24th [[President of the United States|president of the United States]] (1885–1889; 1893–1897). He was the first Democrat elected president after the [[American Civil War|Civil War]] and the first U.S. president to serve nonconsecutive terms. Leader of the Bourbon Democrats, a pro-business movement opposed to high tariffs and free silver, he won the popular vote in 1888 but lost the electoral college to [[Benjamin Harrison|Benjamin Harrison]]. In his second term he faced the Panic of 1893 and intervened in the 1894 Pullman Strike. After leaving office, he joined the American Anti-Imperialist League in protest of the [[Spanish–American War|Spanish–American War]].

Order of [[Bird|birds]] with many living and extinct families. The name means "crane form". Traditionally, wading and terrestrial families that did not fit any other order were grouped here, including 15 species of large [[Crane (bird)|cranes]] and about 145 species of smaller crakes and [[Rail (bird)|rails]]. Recent studies show that these "odd Gruiformes" are at most loosely related to the cranes and rails. The core group, the suborder Grues, comprises rails, flufftails, finfoots, trumpeters, limpkins and cranes. Bustards, seriemas, button-quails and other families represent distinct lineages. Many families known only from [[Fossil|fossils]] have been assigned to the order, but none can be confidently linked to the core group.

City (pop., 2020: 1,385,629), capital of Jalisco state in western Mexico. It has the second-highest population density in Mexico, with over 10,361 people per km², surpassed only by [[Mexico City|Mexico City]]. Its metropolitan area had 5,268,642 people in 2020, the third-largest in Mexico. A settlement was founded here in 1532, and the city moved several times before settling on its current site in 1542. In 1810 [[Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla|Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla]] set up Mexico's first revolutionary government here during the [[Mexican War of Independence|Mexican War of Independence]]. The city hosts the [[Film festival|Guadalajara International Film Festival]], one of the most important in [[Latin America|Latin America]], and the Guadalajara International Book Fair, the largest book fair in the Americas.

Allied offensive against Japan in the [[Solomon Islands|Solomon Islands]] during [[World War II|World War II]]. Fought from August 7, 1942, to February 9, 1943, it was the first major Allied land offensive against Japan. U.S. Marines landed on Guadalcanal, Tulagi and Florida Island, and the Allies completed Henderson Field. Naval battles included Savo Island and the Santa Cruz Islands, culminating in a decisive Allied victory at the Naval Battle of Guadalcanal in November. The campaign marked the Allies' shift from defense to offense and gave them the strategic initiative in the [[Pacific War|Pacific]]. In December, Japan decided to abandon the island.

Overseas department and region of [[France|France]] (pop., 2024: 395,726) in the [[Lesser Antilles|Lesser Antilles]]. It consists of six inhabited islands, 30 uninhabited islets and three inhabited islets. The capital is Basse-Terre, on Basse-Terre Island; the most populous city is Les Abymes, and the main business center is Pointe-à-Pitre, both on Grande-Terre. As a constituent territory of the [[European Union|European Union]], it uses the euro, and EU citizens may settle and work there freely, but it is not part of the [[Schengen Area|Schengen Area]]. Saint Barthélemy and Saint Martin were detached in 2007 after a 2003 referendum. [[Christopher Columbus|Christopher Columbus]] visited in 1493. Guadeloupean Creole is the native language, while French is official and spoken by 84% of the population. Slavery was abolished in 1848. The economy depends on French subsidies, tourism and agriculture, mainly bananas and sugar.

U.S. territory in [[Micronesia|Micronesia]] (pop., 2026: 170,476), largest of the Mariana Islands. Guam is an organized, unincorporated territory, and its capital is Hagåtña. Chamorros are its largest ethnic group but a minority on the multiethnic island. The Chamorro people settled Guam about 3,500 years ago. [[Ferdinand Magellan|Ferdinand Magellan]], sailing for Spain, was the first European to visit and claim it, in 1521. Spain fully colonized the island in 1668. The United States captured Guam during the [[Spanish–American War|Spanish–American War]] in 1898. Japanese forces seized the island on December 8, 1941, and occupied it for two and a half years until American forces recaptured it in July 1944. Tourism and the U.S. military underpin the economy. Guam is one of the 17 non-self-governing territories listed by the [[United Nations|United Nations]].

Wild [[South America|South American]] camelid, closely related to the [[Llama|llama]]. Guanacos are one of two wild South American camelids, the other being the [[Vicuña|vicuña]], which lives at higher elevations. The name comes from the Quechua word wanaku. They stand 1.0 to 1.3 m at the shoulder and weigh 90 to 140 kg, with coats ranging from light brown to dark cinnamon. They are herbivores that graze on grasses, shrubs, herbs, lichens and cacti, and are often found at altitudes up to 4,000 m. Their blood is rich in [[Red blood cell|red blood cells]]: a teaspoon holds about 68 million, four times as many as in a human. Guanaco fiber is prized for its soft, warm feel and is valued second only to vicuña wool. Estimates from 2016 put their numbers at 1.5 to 2 million, mainly in Argentina and Chile.

Coastal province in South China (pop., 2026: 128.590 million). Its capital is [[Guangzhou|Guangzhou]], on the north shore of the [[South China Sea|South China Sea]]. Guangdong has the largest provincial economy in China, with a GDP of CN¥14.16 trillion in 2024, about 10.5 percent of mainland China's output. The [[Pearl River|Pearl River]] Delta Economic Zone is a core for high technology, manufacturing and international trade; within it, [[Shenzhen|Shenzhen]] was China's first special economic zone. [[Hong Kong|Hong Kong]], to the south, is a major financial hub. Guangdong surpassed Henan and Shandong in January 2005 to become China's most populous province. It was the birthplace of [[Sun Yat-sen|Sun Yat-sen]], and its [[Cantonese|Cantonese]] language and cuisine have spread through [[Southeast Asia|Southeast Asia]] and beyond.

Capital and largest city of Guangdong province in southern China. Located on the [[Pearl River|Pearl River]] about 120 km northwest of [[Hong Kong|Hong Kong]], Guangzhou has a history of over 2,200 years and was a major terminus of the [[Silk Road|Silk Road]]. For a long time it was the only Chinese port open to Europeans, and it is also known as Canton. The British captured it during the [[First Opium War|First Opium War]], and it lost trade to Hong Kong and [[Shanghai|Shanghai]], but remained a major entrepôt. The city lies at the center of the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macau Greater Bay Area, an urban agglomeration of about 70 million residents. Its administrative area had a registered population of 18,676,605 in 2020. The annual Canton Fair is the oldest and largest trade fair in China. Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport briefly became the world's busiest by passenger traffic in 2020.

Accumulated excrement of [[Seabird|seabirds]] or [[Bat|bats]], valued as fertilizer. Guano is rich in nitrogen, [[Phosphate|phosphate]] and [[Potassium|potassium]], and was also sought for the production of [[Gunpowder|gunpowder]]. The 19th-century seabird guano trade helped develop modern input-intensive farming and drove the colonization of remote bird islands. Unsustainable mining has killed millions of seabirds. Many cave ecosystems depend wholly on bat guano for nutrients, so losing bats can cause the [[Extinction|extinction]] of dependent species. Chile still mines guano, producing 2,091 to 4,601 metric tons a year in 2014–2023.

East Asian name for the [[Avalokiteśvara|Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara]], associated with compassion. The name is short for Guanshiyin, meaning "Perceiver of the Sounds of the World". Regarded as male in Indian Buddhism, Guanyin has been more commonly depicted as female in China and most of East Asia since about the 12th century. Guanyin is also incorporated into [[Taoism|Taoism]] and [[Chinese folk religion|Chinese folk religion]]. Often called the "most widely beloved Buddhist Divinity", Guanyin is honored at major temples across East Asia. Mount Putuo in [[Zhejiang|Zhejiang]] is the main pilgrimage site in China. Statues of Guanyin are a widely depicted subject in Asian art.

Country in northern [[Central America|Central America]]. The territory was the core of the [[Maya civilization|Maya civilization]], most of which Spain conquered in the 16th century. Guatemala became independent in 1821 and was later ruled by a series of dictators backed by the United States. A 1944 pro-democratic military coup began a decade-long revolution of social and economic reform, which a U.S.-backed military coup ended in 1954. From 1960 to 1996 a civil war between the government and leftist rebels saw massacres of the Maya population by the military, which have been internationally recognized as acts amounting to genocide. A peace accord negotiated by the United Nations in 1996 was followed by economic growth and democratic elections. With an estimated 17.6 million people, Guatemala is the most populous country in Central America. Its capital is [[Guatemala City|Guatemala City]]. Agricultural exports include coffee, bananas and sugar.

National capital and largest city of [[Guatemala|Guatemala]]. The city lies in the Valle de la Ermita, a mountain valley in the south-central part of the country. The Maya city of Kaminaljuyu, occupied primarily between 1500 BCE and 1200 CE, was nearby; its ceremonial center is now a park in the city. Spanish colonists founded the present city after the 1773 Santa Marta earthquake destroyed their colonial capital, Antigua Guatemala. The city was the site of the Act of Independence of Central America, declared in September 1821. It became the national capital in 1847, when Guatemala declared itself an independent republic. The 1917–1918 earthquakes destroyed much of the city, and reconstruction brought wider streets and a grid layout. Its metropolitan area is the largest in Central America.

Tropical fruit of a small tree in the [[Myrtaceae|myrtle family]]. Botanically, guavas are berries. The common guava, Psidium guajava, is native to Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and northern South America, and is grown in many tropical and subtropical regions. Archaeological sites in Peru show guava cultivation as early as 2500 BC. In 2024, world production of guavas, combined with mangos and mangosteens, was 62 million metric tons, led by [[India|India]] with 45%. Introduced to Florida in the 19th century, guavas are a primary host of the Caribbean fruit fly. In [[Hawaii|Hawaii]], the strawberry guava has become an aggressive [[Invasive species|invasive species]]. Trees grown from seed can bear fruit in two years and continue to do so for 40 years.

Largest city and main port of [[Ecuador|Ecuador]], capital of Guayas Province. Established in 1535 as a shipyard and port in service of the [[Spanish Empire|Spanish Empire]], it became a key trade hub of the colony. Guayaquil was the first Ecuadorian city to achieve independence from Spain, on October 9, 1820. It later was part of [[Gran Colombia|Gran Colombia]] and has been part of the Republic of Ecuador since 1830. The port is one of the most important on the eastern Pacific coast, handling about 70% of the country's private exports and 83% of its imports. With more than 3,000,000 people, it is the most populous urban agglomeration in Ecuador. Together with [[Quito|Quito]], the national capital, it is one of the country's two main development poles.

Rival factions in medieval Italy, supporting the [[Pope|pope]] (Guelphs) or the [[Holy Roman Empire|Holy Roman Emperor]] (Ghibellines). Their rivalry dominated Italian politics in the 12th and 13th centuries and grew from the [[Investiture Controversy|Investiture Controversy]], which began in 1075 and ended with the Concordat of Worms in 1122. "Guelph" derives from the House of Welf, dukes of [[Bavaria|Bavaria]]; "Ghibelline" derives from Waiblingen, a Hohenstaufen rallying cry. Cities threatened by the expansion of the [[Papal States|Papal States]] tended to be Ghibelline, while cities seeking autonomy from the empire tended to be Guelph. Alignments were often local: Guelph Florence and Ghibelline Siena fought at Montaperti in 1260. Factions differed from guild to guild, and cities could change sides. The conflicts ended in the late 14th century.

Large 1937 anti-war [[Oil painting|oil painting]] by Spanish artist [[Pablo Picasso|Pablo Picasso]]. Picasso painted *Guernica* in Paris in response to the April 26, 1937, bombing of the Basque town of Guernica by aircraft of [[Nazi Germany|Nazi Germany]]'s Condor Legion and the fascist government of Italy, during the [[Spanish Civil War|Spanish Civil War]]. The grey, black and white canvas, 3.49 m by 7.76 m, shows grieving women, a gored horse, a bull, a dead dove, a dead baby and flames. Many art critics regard it as the most moving and powerful anti-war painting in history. It was shown at the Spanish pavilion of the 1937 Paris International Exposition and then toured to raise funds for Spanish war relief. It is now housed in the Museo Reina Sofía in [[Madrid|Madrid]].

Second-largest of the [[Channel Islands|Channel Islands]] (pop., 2023: 64,781), in the [[English Channel|English Channel]] off Normandy. It is the main island of the Bailiwick of Guernsey, a self-governing British Crown dependency that is not part of the [[United Kingdom|United Kingdom]]. Its legislature is the States of Guernsey. Financial services is the largest industry, followed by tourism and agriculture. [[Nazi Germany|Nazi Germany]] occupied Guernsey during World War II, and it was liberated on May 9, 1945. [[Victor Hugo|Victor Hugo]] spent 15 years in exile there and wrote some of his best-known works. The island uses the [[Pound sterling|pound sterling]].

Italian radio-frequency engineer and inventor. Marconi developed a practical wireless telegraph system based on [[Radio wave|radio waves]], which led to his being largely credited as the inventor of [[Radio|radio]]. He shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Ferdinand Braun for contributions to wireless telegraphy. Building on the 1888 demonstration by [[Heinrich Hertz|Heinrich Hertz]] that [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]] could be produced and detected, he worked on wireless telegraphy from the early 1890s. In 1897 he founded the Wireless Telegraph & Signal Company in the [[United Kingdom|United Kingdom]], later the Marconi Company. On December 12, 1901, he received the first transatlantic radio signal, the Morse letter "S", sent from Poldhu, [[Cornwall|Cornwall]], to St. John's, Newfoundland. In 1929 he was made a marquess, and in 1931 he set up Vatican Radio for Pope Pius XI.

Precambrian geological formation in northeast [[South America|South America]]. It is one of the three cratons of the South American plate and is about 1.7 billion years old. The shield underlies [[Guyana|Guyana]], [[Suriname|Suriname]], [[French Guiana|French Guiana]], much of southern [[Venezuela|Venezuela]], most of [[Brazil|Brazil]] north of the [[Amazon River|Amazon River]], and parts of eastern Colombia. Its higher elevations, the Guiana Highlands, hold flat-topped tepuis and are the source of waterfalls such as [[Angel Falls|Angel Falls]], Kaieteur Falls and Cuquenan Falls. The highest point is Pico da Neblina in Brazil, at 2,995 m (9,826 ft). The shield is one of the world's most biodiverse regions, with over 3,000 vertebrate species, including 1,168 freshwater fish and 269 amphibians. About 13,367 vascular plant species have been found, approximately 40% of them endemic.
